analytic.title: Reconfiguration-aware Real-Time Scheduling under QoS Constraint

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Due to the increase in demand for reconfigurability in embedded systems, schedulability in real-time task scheduling is challenged by non-negligible reconfiguration overheads. Reconfiguration of the system during task execution affects both deadline miss rate and deadline miss distribution. On the other hand, Quality of Service (QoS) in several embedded applications is not only determined by deadline miss rate but also the distribution of the tasks missing their deadlines (known as weakly-hard real-time systems). As a result, we propose to model QoS constraints as a set of constraints on dropout patterns (due to reconfiguration overhead) and present a novel online solution for the problem of reconfiguration-aware real-time scheduling. According to QoS constraints, we divide the ready instances of the tasks into two groups: critical and non-critical, then model each group as a network flow problem and provide an online scheduler for each group. We deployed our method on synthetic benchmarks as well as software defined radio implementation of VoIP on reconfigurable systems. Results show that our solution reduces the number of QoS violations by 19.01 times and 2.33 times (57.02%) in comparison with Bi-Modal Scheduler (BMS) [1] for synthetic benchmarks with low and high QoS constraint, respectively.

div.head: I. Introduction
div.p: There is an extensive increase in demand for embedded systems in recent years. Many of these embedded systems require flexibility and adaptation during execution. Although processor-based implementation provides ultimate flexibility, computationally intensive processing in the system mandates hardware support in addition to the processors. Reconfigurable hardware is a promising solution since it provides reconfigurability, yet high performance computing. The main drawback of reconfigurable hardware platform is delay overhead during reconfiguration. This delay overhead can be the time to reconfigure a reconfigurable processor (soft processor), processor with reconfigurable coprocessors and/or memory, or a reconfigurable hardware (fine or coarse grained). If this overhead is not negligible, it challenges the real-time scheduling and it will affect the quality of service (QoS) of the system.

There has been increasing interest in real-time schedulers for QoS-based systems. Mostly defined in multimedia and telecommunication systems, QoS should be within a valid range. Otherwise, the deadline misses can affect the quality of application. The commonly used QoS metric is the deadline miss rate, defined as the percentage of the number of deadline misses with respect to the number of jobs admitted to the system. However, the drawback of this metric is that they cannot directly express how deadline missed are distributed. In many systems, perceptible performance is sensitive to dropout pattern and the distribution of dropouts. So if we can control the dropout patterns caused by reconfiguration overhead and plan for them ahead of time, we can prevent QoS degradation significantly.

In this paper, we consider weakly-hard real time systems [2] in which deadline misses can be tolerated under specific distribution patterns. Based on the QoS constraint, the tasks are categorized into two groups: critical and non-critical. A critical job (We call each invocation of a task, a job of that task) is a job whose deadline if missed results in a QoS violation. Non-critical jobs are the jobs which can be dropped without violating the QoS constraint.

In this paper, we present an online reconfiguration-aware scheduler for weakly-hard real time systems. For critical jobs, we satisfy the QoS constraint. For non-critical jobs, we consider the reconfiguration overhead between the tasks. If there were enough slack time for non-important jobs (i.e. the jobs that can be dropped without violating the QoS), we will schedule them. Since reconfiguration overhead is dependent on the current job on the processing element and the next job, changing the ordering of the tasks will change the overhead. So to find the proper ordering of the task execution, we model the task ordering as finding a path.

We validate our technique by simulating synthetic benchmarks as well as a VoIP application as a case study. We compared our scheduler with an EDF-based QoS-aware scheduler (Bi-Modal Scheduler) [1]. Results show that in benchmarks with low QoS constraint, we improved the number of QoS violations by 19.01 times and in benchmarks with high QoS constraint we improved the number of QoS violations by 2.33 times (57.02%), on average. In VoIP benchmarks, we improved the number of dropped calls by 8.58%, on average.

div.head: II. Related Works
div.p: To overcome the shortcoming of the QoS metrics based on average dropout rate, a variety of window-based QoS constraints have been proposed for firm-deadline real-time systems. (m,k)-firm constraint is presented in [3]. This constraint specifies that tasks are desired to meet m deadlines in any k consecutive invocations. One problem with this approach is that they assumed that all the tasks have the same m, k parameters. Another approach is the introduction of skip factor in [4]. If a task has a skip factor of s, it will have one invocation skipped out of s. The drawback of this approach is that every s task invocations; one is skipped even if it meets the deadline when scheduled. Bernat et al. [2] introduced the notion of weakly-hard real-time constraints as a generalization of the concept of (m,k)-firm to cover other types of dropout patterns. None of the abovementioned related work considers the transition overhead during task switching.
Several research works focus on real-time task scheduling on

div.head: 2A-4
div.p: reconfigurable hardwares, but transition overhead is either ignored [5,6] or considered as a constant [7,8]. There is a work [9] which considers the transition-overhead during static task scheduling but the objective is minimizing the deadline miss rate.

div.head: III. Target SoC Platform
div.p: In this paper we target a platform consisting of a Processing Element (PE) which can be a reconfigurable processor (soft processor), processor with reconfigurable coprocessors and/or memory, or a reconfigurable hardware (fine or coarse grained). The PE can be reconfigured/updated during runtime (i.e. dynamic reconfiguration). The configuration bitstreams of each task is stored in a Configuration Library and the Reconfiguration Manager forces the PE to reconfigure appropriately, based on the task schedule received from the scheduler (Figure 1). Reconfiguration overhead is the time needed to reconfigure the new task on the PE. The input to this system is a set of periodic real-time tasks with their QoS constraints modeled in terms of acceptable deadline miss rates and patterns. Based on the reconfiguration overhead information calculated from Configuration Bitstream Library and the timing requirement of the tasks, the Scheduler schedules the tasks on the PE.

div.head: IV. Real-time Scheduling
div.p: We are given a set of periodic tasks, ={ i }. Each periodic task i is characterized by a quadruple (p i , d i , e i , i ). p i is the period, d i is the relative deadline, e i is the execution time and i is QoS constraint (this parameter captures the deadline miss rates as well as the patterns). Between each pair of tasks there is a reconfiguration overhead, R ij , which is known a priori.

In this section we will present the important components of our real-time scheduler: a) QoS Model: In order to capture the QoS of an individual task under different dropout rates and patterns, we need a QoS model. b) Criticality Function: We need a function to indicate how far a task is from violating its QoS constraint. Or in other words, how critical is the current job of a task. c) Reconfiguration-aware Online Scheduler: This is the core component of our scheduler which schedules tasks based on their timings, QoS criticalities and the reconfiguration overheads.

div.head: A. QoS Model
div.p: The tolerance to missed deadlines cannot be adequately specified by a single parameter, for example with the percentage of deadlines to be met or missed. This is because, in general, such requirements only represent average information over a large period of time. For example "10% of deadline can be missed" may mean one deadline is missed every 10 task invocations or it may mean that 100 deadlines may be missed followed by 900 deadlines met, which is clearly not the same.

To capture this situation another parameter describing the window of the time within which the number of deadlines must hold should be specified. This window can be categorized as two types: 1) Fixed-window constraint, where adjacent windows do not have overlap with each other. 2) Sliding-window constraint, where the window slides along the time line. Since the fixed-window constraint is a subset of sliding-window constraint, we are considering sliding-window constraint in our paper.

There are some works in literature considering the sliding-window QoS constraint which make scheduling decisions based on dropout rates and patterns. In this paper we adopt the technique in [1] which is one of the most general and powerful online algorithms for window-based constraints. There are four types of QoS constraint ( ) described in this paper. div.head: B. Criticality Function
div.p: When a job of a task is in the scheduler ready queue, one of the following two states is assigned to it based on its QoS constraint:
Critical State: if the current job must be scheduled in order to prevent violating its QoS constraint.
Non-Critical State: if the current job could be dropped without jeopardizing the satisfaction of the QoS constraint.

To find the state of a new job, the criticality of it should be calculated by a Criticality Function ( ). This function determines the number of consecutive successive deadlines that a task can miss without violating its QoS constraint. So if this value is zero for a given job, the corresponding task is in critical state (i.e. the job should be executed), otherwise it is in non-critical state. For more information you can refer to [1].

div.head: C. Reconfiguration-aware Online Scheduler
div.p: After we find the state for each ready job, we need to schedule the critical ones and if there was enough time we start scheduling the non-critical jobs. To schedule each group of jobs, we run our reconfiguration-aware scheduler. To do so, we model the jobs as a set of customers in a graph. Each customer represents the execution of a job on the PE. There is a set of edges between customers where each edge represents a reconfiguration sequence of two consecutive jobs on the PE. Let's assume that the current job on the PE is j 0 , and there are three new jobs arriving (j 1 , j 2 , j 3 ). The graph modeling this case is shown in Figure 2. The edge labeled R 01 represents the execution of j 1 after j 0 on the PE.

Each customer in the system is associated with the execution time of the corresponding job (e i ) and the time window that the job must start in order to meet its deadline ([a i ,b i ]). This window can be calculated based on the period, deadline and the execution of the task. For example the time window for n-th job

There is a start time (t i ) associated with each customer i and as long as the start time of the customer lies within the corresponding time window of the customer, the job represented by that customer is feasibly scheduled. We need to create a path constructed by customers which shows the order of execution of the jobs on a PE. For example in Figure 2, the path constructed by R 01 , R 13 , R 32 represents the execution of j 1 after the current job, then executing j 3 and j 2 on the PE. This problem is similar to Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Window (VRPTW). In this problem there are a set of customers with a time window to be served and a vehicle to serve these customers within their time window for a predefined service time. The solution belongs to the class of sequential, tour-building algorithms. In each iteration, the insertion algorithm finds the appropriate unscheduled customer and inserts it in the best place in the partial path (in terms of a measure to be described later). We add look-ahead ability to our scheduler for non-critical jobs and introduce the concept of safe window to improve the results. The goal is to create the path using the jobs in the safe window and after the path is created we start scheduling the jobs using the guideline of the path.

We have two schedulers in our algorithm. The first one is the scheduler for critical jobs and the second one is the scheduler for non-critical jobs. Each scheduler performs three steps: 1) find the set of possible candidate customers to insert into the path 2) find the best customer from the set to insert in the path 3) find the best place for the candidate to be inserted in the partial path.

div.head: Scheduler for Critical Jobs
div.p: In this case, at least one of the tasks is in critical state. We intend to create a set CJ (Critical Jobs) which contains all the candidates for insertion. At each time, CJ contains all the critical jobs in the ready queue. For example in Figure 2, if new job1 and job2 are critical but job3 is normal, CJ will only contain j 1 and j 2 .

To find the best customer to insert, we find the job with the earliest deadline in CJ. This job is the most critical job in CJ (the same idea as EDF), so we pick this job as the best customer at each step.

For finding the best place to insert the picked customer, we use a metric based on [10]. The method uses the criteria c(i, u, j) to insert a new unrouted customer u into the partial path, between two adjacent customers i and j on the path. Let (i 0 , i 1 ,…, i m ) be the current path. div.head: Scheduler for Non-Critical Jobs
div.p: If no job in the ready queue is in critical state, we use our second scheduler. We introduce the concept of safe window in this case. If there is no critical job in the ready queue, we can look ahead for the earliest critical job among different tasks (assuming all the non-critical jobs are dropped). The time between the current time and the arrival time of that job is the safe window (Figure 3), because any decision we make for the jobs in this window will not result in violating the QoS 2A-4 constraint (i.e. all the jobs in the safe window are non-critical and dropping them will not violate the QoS constraint). If a non-critical job starts inside the safe window and it can be finished before ending the safe window it is considered inside the safe window. These jobs are stored in a set named NCJ (Non-Critical Jobs) which is the set of candidates for insertion in next steps.

In this scheduler the basic idea is to create a path using the customers and then to use the path to guide the scheduler for scheduling the jobs. The criterion while creating the path is to extend the safe window as much as possible.

In order to find the best customer to insert at each step, we find the earliest critical job of each task. The earlier is the critical job of a task, the more critical it is to schedule the task. So we always sort the tasks based on the arrival time of their critical job and try to insert a customer from the task with the earliest critical job (i.e. most critical task) into the partial path in order to postpone the earliest critical job and potentially extend the safe window. The job that should be chosen is the latest unscheduled job of the most critical task that can be feasibly inserted in the partial path (the critical job can only be postponed if we schedule a job from the corresponding task and the latest unscheduled job of that task has the maximum increase in the criticality function).

There is a slight difference between the process of creating a path in this scheduler and the path creation in scheduler for critical jobs. In this case we choose a job as a seed in the first step and then insert other jobs in the best place before this job. The seed is the job exactly before the earliest critical job (from the same task). We choose this job as the seed because executing this job will definitely extend the safe window (the earliest critical job was found with the assumption that all the non-critical jobs are dropped and now one of them is not dropped) and if we update the safe window we need to run the path creation again. So we don't add any job after the seed because we will consider them in the next safe window. So after the seed is inserted, NCJ only contains the jobs that can be inserted before the seed. If in some step it is not possible to postpone the earliest critical job, we ignore the task and we check the task with the next earliest critical job.

For example, Figure 3 shows a safe window and the highlighted jobs are contained in NCJ. j 1 is the latest job in the safe window before the earliest critical job (cj 0 ) from the same task. We select this job as the seed and insert in the path. By inserting this job in the path, the earliest critical job will be postponed. So the next earliest critical job will be cj 1 and we insert j 2 . By postponing the critical job of task1, the earliest critical job will be cj 2 . At this time, we need to insert the latest job of task2 before the seed so we choose j 3 for insertion and this process will continue. The index of the jobs shows the order of insertion in the partial path.

Finding the best place to insert the best customer is by using the same equations ( 1)-( 4). After we insert the seed, other customers are inserted before this seed and this will automatically happen because NCJ only contains the jobs before the seed.

If n is the number of jobs to schedule at each step, the order of algorithm for finding the best customer to insert in the path is O(nlogn) because in both cases it is just a sorting and finding the minimum number. The order of algorithm to insert in the best place with feasibility check is O(n 2 ) because at the worst case we need to check n different places in the partial path and to check each place, on average, we need to check n/2 customers after that place for feasibility after new customer insertion. So the overall time of finding and inserting a customer in the path is O(n 2 ) and since at the worst, this should be done for each job at each step, the order of algorithm is O(n 3 ) which is a polynomial execution time and it is small enough for an online scheduler, considering that, the set of candidate nodes for insertion during path construction (n) is small.

We have two policies when a QoS violation happens. In the first policy, if a critical job is dropped (i.e. QoS violation for one task happens), the whole task is dropped and it's not continued anymore. In the second policy, although a QoS violation is happened, we will continue that task and the QoS violation may be temporary.

div.head: V. Case Study: Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP)
div.p: In this section we explain the usage of our technique in VoIP application on Software Defined Radio (SDR). SDR [11] is a platform for coexistence of heterogeneous wireless systems over a common ISM carrier, in order to increase the spectrum utilization. In SDRs, a wide variety of strategies and protocols can be implemented in software and the same spectrum can be shared. Reconfigurable hardware platforms are promising to implement SDR, since it is not efficient to implement all the different protocols on a chip at the same time. In addition, reconfiguration allows feature changes in the hardware if the communication protocols in the SDR system are updated.

In this paper we are assuming an FPGA-based SDR where multiple communication support is realized through runtime reconfiguration of the FPGA device. We deploy our scheduler for time slot allocation to protocols while considering transition delay overhead of underlying hardware. We do our experiments on the physical layer implementation for 4 different protocols. These protocols are very similar to WiFi, WiMax, GPRS and WCDMA. A set of distinctive and important components of these protocols like Turbo Enc/Dec, RS Enc/Dec, FFT/IFFT, etc are implemented on the target FPGA.

The FPGA architecture that we have assumed for our benchmarks is Virtex 4 architecture. Reconfiguration time overhead includes the time ICAP fetches the configuration bits and reconfigures the FPGA device. This delay for one configuration frame is the same across all V4 devices and is equal to 13.1us for one frame. We apply hardware reuse and configuration prefetch during the reconfiguration overhead computations.

The VoIP SDR is a system where several VoIP calls with various codecs share the same hardware. Each call has a QoS constraint in terms of quality of speech. The metric to measure the quality in VoIP applications is Mean Opinion Score (MOS) which is based on subjective tests.
